page_summary:
Writing to Eugene Warren after returning from a trip to Metz, France -- where he delivered a speech on heavy theology that a local paper reported under the headline 'For Philip K. Dick the concept of God is not sufficient!' and where he formed a brief, wistful, unconsummated attachment to a young French woman he never learned the surname of -- Dick describes seeing the French premiere of Star Wars and being struck by its 'theological implications.' He quotes several passages from the novelization describing 'the Force' as an omnipresent energy field that both controls and obeys, and argues that this description closely resembles the plasmatic entity (which he calls VALIS or Zebra) that took him over during his March 1974 religious experience -- down to the detail of the character Luke hearing the voice of the dead Obi-Wan Kenobi, paralleling Dick's own claim to have heard the voice of the risen Christ. He speculates that George Lucas may be unconsciously channeling genuine theological truth to a mass audience, delivering 'the Word' through popular culture ('up... from the gutter,' as he says he had already depicted the divine Word arriving via television commercials in Ubik) rather than through traditional religious channels, and closes with a postscript affirming his belief that the 1974 experience was the Holy Spirit, comparing his own religious writing's modest reach favorably against Lucas's vastly larger audience as evidence that God works through whatever channel -- however secular -- can actually reach people.

**Why it matters.** The letter is a striking example of Dick's tendency, well documented across his post-1974 correspondence and the Exegesis, to find confirmation of his religious experience nearly everywhere in contemporary culture -- here in a science-fiction blockbuster's invented mythology rather than in scripture or philosophy. His explicit self-comparison to Lucas ('What I myself have done is a mere tittle in comparison to what Lucas has done') frames the letter's argument charitably rather than competitively: both men, in Dick's view, serve as instruments delivering the same underlying truth to different scales of audience, with Lucas's popular success read as evidence of God's practical strategy for reaching a 'secular' modern public rather than as a rival claim to Dick's own more esoteric religious writing. The letter's juxtaposition of high theology with a plainly personal, unresolved travel romance gives an unusually intimate view of how thoroughly the two registers coexisted in Dick's daily correspondence during this period.

*Dick's handwritten postscript notation -- a reminder to himself about an upcoming Good Morning America appearance -- closes the letter on an abrupt note of ordinary media-career logistics, immediately after several paragraphs of sustained theological argument.*

structure.form: personal letter in three movements: a lost-letter apology and a wistful travel narrative, an extended theological reading of Star Wars, and a postscript restating Dick's own religious convictions
movements: Dick apologizes for having lost Warren's previous letter, then recounts his trip to Metz, France -- a theologically-charged speech, a brief unconsummated romance, and his ambivalence about returning to Southern California.

He describes seeing Star Wars in France and quotes several passages describing 'the Force,' arguing it closely parallels the plasmatic entity (VALIS/Zebra) from his own 1974 experience, down to a dead mentor's voice guiding the protagonist.

A postscript affirms his belief that his 1974 experience was the Holy Spirit, and proposes that George Lucas -- consciously or not -- is delivering genuine theological truth to a mass audience through popular film, just as Dick says he anticipated in Ubik with the divine Word arriving through vulgar TV commercials.
structure.point_of_view: first person, Dick writing intimately and digressively to a trusted correspondent, moving without much transition between personal travel anecdote and extended theological argument.
structure.central_device: A popular science-fiction film's invented mythology ('the Force') is read not as fiction resembling Dick's experience by coincidence, but as independent, possibly unconscious confirmation of it -- turning a fan's enthusiastic close-reading of a blockbuster into a theological argument about how divine truth reaches a secular mass audience.

characters.name: Philip K. Dick (letter-writer)
characters.note: Moves fluidly between deep personal vulnerability (his account of the unnamed French woman, his dread of returning to California) and confident theological argument, treating both registers as equally serious within the same letter.

characters.name: Eugene Warren
characters.note: A trusted correspondent to whom Dick had apparently already sent enough personal letters that Warren had asked permission to show them to friends -- indicating an established, ongoing epistolary relationship rather than a first contact.

characters.name: George Lucas
characters.note: Never contacted or quoted directly; Dick speculates about his intentions and unconscious motivations entirely from the outside, concluding that Lucas is instrumentally serving a divine purpose regardless of his own awareness of it.

settings.name: Metz, France
settings.note: The site of Dick's theologically-charged public speech, his brief romantic encounter, and his viewing of the French premiere of Star Wars -- rendered with genuine longing as a place of adventure and excitement in explicit contrast to his dread of returning to 'awful' Southern California.

motifs: A popular cultural artifact (a blockbuster film) read as unconscious or providential confirmation of a private religious experience
Divine truth arriving through debased or secular channels ('up... from the gutter') rather than through traditional religious authority
A creator's own awareness or intention treated as irrelevant to whether their work serves a genuine theological purpose
Travel and romantic longing (Metz, the unnamed French woman) as a counterpoint of ordinary, unresolved human desire alongside cosmic theological speculation

pkd_on_this_work.summary: This entire document is Dick's own first-person testimony; there is no separate 'commentary on it' to distinguish from the work itself.

evidence.source: The Selected Letters of Philip K. Dick, 1977-1979
evidence.quote: the description of "the force" in STAR WARS for unaccountable reasons resembles the entity or force which took me over during my religious experiences in March of 1974
evidence.reading: States directly Dick's own central claim connecting the film to his 1974 experience.

open_questions: Did Eugene Warren ever publish or discuss his correspondence with Dick specifically regarding this letter's Star Wars argument?
Is this letter's identification of VALIS/Zebra with 'the Force' discussed anywhere in scholarship on Dick's engagement with contemporary popular culture as a source of theological confirmation?
How does this letter's comparatively generous, non-competitive framing of Lucas's success compare to Dick's attitude toward other contemporaries' commercial success elsewhere in his correspondence?

reading_provenance.note: Close reading of the primary text plus attributed evidence from the archive. Candidate: not yet promoted to canonical.

critical_caution: This is a personal letter, not fiction or an essay -- Dick writing in his own voice to a specific real recipient (Eugene Warren) about seeing Star Wars in France and connecting it to his 1974 religious experience. It is classified under lane E (Dick's own testimony) in full; the 'reading' fields below describe the letter's actual autobiographical content, not an invented plot.
